strengths: Well-motivated approach addressing real limitation of existing distillation methods with clear intuition that step-to-step gaps are smaller than teacher-student gaps
Strong experimental results especially on extreme few-step scenarios (1-2 steps): 3.27 point improvement at 1-step, 96% user preference over Self-Forcing
Practical step-unified model design supporting multiple inference-step configurations without requiring separate re-distillation
Insightful empirical analysis (Figure 4) showing first frames have lower similarity across denoising steps, motivating FFE strategy
Comprehensive evaluation including VBench metrics, user studies with 20 prompts, thorough ablations clearly demonstrating component contributions (Table 2)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations explaining the ASD approach and demonstrating improvements across inference settings
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: ASD is straightforward extension of existing adversarial distillation methods (ADD, SDXL-Lightning, LADD); FFE is simple heuristic with no deep insights; no theoretical analysis or convergence guarantees
Highly incremental over very recent concurrent work (Self-Forcing 2025, DMD 2024); minimal improvement at standard settings (84.38 vs 84.31 at 4-step showing only 0.07 point gain)

FFE dominates improvements at extreme few-step settings (Table 2: FFE alone ~4.9 points vs ASD ~2.5 points at 1-step), yet FFE is post-hoc inference strategy rather than core distillation contribution
Narrow experimental scope: only text-to-video, single 1.3B model size, one resolution (832×480); no speed/latency measurements; limited to one base architecture
Fair comparisons at 1-2 steps required authors to retrain Self-Forcing themselves (Self-Forcing†), limiting independent validation of claimed improvements
Shallow analysis: limited investigation into why ASD works; arbitrary FFE design choices (T=4, R) without ablation; no failure case analysis; missing discussion of when FFE helps most/least
Hyperparameter sensitivity shown in Figure 8 at 1-step generation; missing details on optimizer, learning rates, training time; reproducibility concerns as code not available

strengths: Clear motivation for self-distillation approach with well-articulated intuition about smaller step-to-step gaps providing smoother supervision
Practical step-unified design that enables a single model to support multiple inference-step settings without retraining
Comprehensive empirical evaluation including quantitative metrics (VBench), human user study, ablation studies, and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis
Strong results in extreme few-step setting: 3.27-point improvement over retrained Self-Forcing and 96% user preference for 1-step generation
Technical soundness with reasonable implementation details and proposed reproducibility materials
weaknesses: Limited novelty: ASD is a straightforward application of existing adversarial distillation to adjacent steps, and FFE is a heuristic inference strategy without theoretical justification

Weak baseline comparisons: improvements at 4-steps are negligible (0.07 pts), and 1-2 step improvements are against retrained Self-Forcing with unclear optimization; no comparison with other recent distillation methods
Critical missing analysis: no computational efficiency metrics (runtime, FLOPs, memory) despite claims of 'extreme limited denoising steps'; what is actual speedup?
Narrow evaluation scope: single task (text-to-video), single architecture (1.3B), single benchmark (VBench only); generalization to other models/tasks unexplored

Technical clarity issues: different random seeds for z1 and z2 in Eq. 4 lack justification; parameter sharing of discriminators only mentioned in implementation; Algorithm 1 step sampling strategy unclear

FFE strategy lacks rigorous justification: similarity patterns (Fig 4) could result from random initialization differences; specific 4-step choice for first frame is arbitrary with no ablation on alternatives
Incomplete user study: only 20 prompts, no inter-annotator agreement or statistical significance testing, number of annotators not specified
Missing critical ablations: no step-unified vs step-specific comparison, no analysis of training cost vs DMD-only, no comparison of step allocations for FFE

strengths: Clear motivation and intuitive solution: The paper effectively articulates why direct teacher-student alignment fails for extreme few-step distillation and proposes a well-motivated alternative through step-wise self-distillation
Strong empirical results: Achieves SOTA on VBench for 1-step and 2-step generation with 96% and 62% user preference over strong Self-Forcing baseline
Practical flexibility: Single unified model supports multiple inference-step configurations without retraining, valuable for deployment scenarios requiring dynamic speed-quality tradeoffs
Empirically-grounded design: First-Frame Enhancement strategy backed by concrete evidence (Figure 4) showing lower similarity in first frames across denoising steps

Comprehensive experimental validation: Thorough ablations quantifying contributions (ASD +2.52, FFE +4.19 on Total Score), user preferences, qualitative comparisons, and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis
Well-structured presentation: Clear exposition with effective visualizations (especially Figure 1) and logical flow
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution combines existing DMD with standard adversarial distillation techniques; individual components (ASD, FFE) are relatively straightforward without introducing fundamentally new concepts
Insufficient theoretical justification: Claims about stability improvements for adjacent-step alignment lack rigorous support; no gradient analysis, loss landscape study, or formal stability proofs
Missing computational analysis: No actual inference time, throughput, or memory measurements provided despite efficiency being a key motivation
Narrow evaluation scope: Only VBench tested; missing other metrics (CLIPSIM, FVD), resolutions, domains (image-to-video), and long-form video despite being cited as motivation
Insufficient mechanistic analysis: No investigation of actual distribution differences between n and (n+1)-step outputs, gradient behavior comparisons, or visualizations of learned distributions
Technical justification gaps: Arbitrary hyperparameters (λ=600, σ=0.05), design choices (shared discriminator backbone) lack explanation; random step selection during training not analyzed
Limited user study: Only 20 prompts may be insufficient to draw strong conclusions about general applicability
Reproducibility concerns: Code unavailable, dependent on large 14B score estimator model, minimal sensitivity analysis for small training batch size (8)
